newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: US Senator says White House out of line on UN Chief.
newsitem.headline: US Senator says White House out of line on UN Chief.

text.p: A U.S. senator on Thursday called the White House opposition to Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali irrational and embarrassing and said there was still time for it to change its mind.

At the same time, Clinton administration aides close to U.S. Ambassador Madeleine Albright accused Boutros-Ghali of telephoning congressmen and thereby interfering in U.S. politics. U.N. spokeswoman Sylvanna Foa denied that the secretary-general had been campaigning for his re-election.
At issue is Boutros-Ghali's bid this year for a second five-year term, which the United States, led by Albright, vows to veto on grounds he has not championed reform of the world body.
African nations say U.S. envoys are warning them they would lose an opportunity to have another secretary-general from their continent if they continued to back the 74-year-old Egyptian.
But Sen. Paul Simon, an Illinois Democrat who is resigning from the Senate this year, said in statements distributed here and in Washington that the United States was making a mistake.
"We are wrong and it is an embarrassment," Simon said. "I hope, with the election over, rational thinking will return to our handling of this situation."

"The assumption is made, accurately, that we are prepared to veto the secretary-general -- the first secretary-general who would not be granted a second term -- either because of domestic political reasons or because he has on rare occasions shown independence from U.S. wishes.
"Either reason is not worthy of a great power," he added. "Greatness suggests something more than a crude use of power."

Consultations in the Security Council begin next week and promises to be drawn out. No one candidate has emerged and France, which like the United States has a veto in the 15-member body, has promised to give Washington a hard time.

In a news conference in Washington, Simon said he believed the U.S. decision "was 95 percent domestic politics and 5 percent because they were unhappy that he was not going along with the United States on a few things."
He said he told Albright, who phoned him before his news conference, that Boutros-Ghali "has cut the budget and reduced the personnel. I think he has done a significant amount."
Simon suggested that perhaps there should be a compromise for a three-year term, but administration officials have rejected this.
Secretary of State Warren Christopher last spring offered Boutros-Ghali a one-year extension but the U.N. chief rejected it and the offer was withdrawn.
"It is still gone," said a Clinton administration official, disputing recent reports that the compromise was still in play.

The aide said that Boutros-Ghali had telephoned Representative Lee Hamilton, an Indiana Democrat, among others, mentioning the Simon press conference but not directly asking for his support. Hamilton then told Albright.

"I don't understand the argument that this is somehow meddling if you talk to democratically elected members of Congress or the Senate," said Simon's spokesman Michael Briggs. "This is a government with three branches."
Part of the problem, he said, was the $1.4 billion debt the United States owed to the United Nations. "And Congress appropriates the money and not the executive branch."
Foa said Boutros-Ghali "is not campaigning and he is not electioneering.

"He has lots of friends in Congress. He has been on the world scene for a long time. I don't think there is any law against taking phone calls," she said. "He might even initiate a phone call. This man does not have time to have a decent breakfast, he does not have time to mess around with frivolous phone calls."
